title: Start with observation
text: Driving safely starts before the manoeuvre. A good driver keeps looking, interprets what is happening and plans early. The aim is not merely to react after a hazard appears, but to notice it soon enough to choose a safe, legal response.

title: Zimbabwe keeps left
text: In Zimbabwe, traffic keeps to the left. On an ordinary two-way road, keep your vehicle on the left side. Moving across the centre is only for a permitted movement, instruction, or situation where the road layout requires it.

title: Mirrors extend your view
text: Mirrors show what is happening behind and beside you. Check them regularly, especially before changing speed, position or direction. A mirror check does not replace a blind-spot check when another road user could be hidden.

title: Look beyond the vehicle ahead
text: The road farther ahead tells you what is developing. Look through gaps where possible instead of staring only at the car immediately in front. Early sight of queues, crossings, junctions and hazards gives you more time to act.

title: Keep an escape space
text: A safe driver preserves options. Leave enough space to brake or steer around a hazard when appropriate. Avoid travelling where another driver's mistake would leave you with no safe response.

title: Smooth inputs improve control
text: Smooth driving makes the vehicle easier to manage. Progressive steering, braking and acceleration keep the vehicle more stable and make your intentions easier for other road users to predict.

title: Speed changes time
text: Higher speed reduces the time available to deal with hazards. You cover more ground every second as speed rises, and stopping generally requires more distance. Choose speed according to the whole road situation, not the speedometer alone.

title: A speed limit is a maximum
text: A posted limit does not tell you the speed you must use. You may need to travel below the limit when visibility, traffic, weather, pedestrians, road surface or vehicle condition make a lower speed necessary.

title: Prepare for bends early
text: The safe speed for a bend is chosen before entry. Slow before a sharp or poorly visible bend so you are settled when steering through it. Entering too fast can leave little room for a stopped vehicle, pedestrian or oncoming road user.

title: Read the road, not just the signs
text: Signs are one part of road information. Road markings, signals, parked vehicles, pedestrian movement, junction layout and changing road surfaces also tell you what is happening. Good driving combines these clues.

title: A familiar road can still change
text: Habit is not a substitute for observation. Road works, pedestrians, parked cars, weather and damaged surfaces can change the risk on a road you know well. Reassess the road every trip.

title: Night reduces useful information
text: Darkness makes some hazards harder to detect. Pedestrians, animals, unlit vehicles and road defects can be less visible at night. Use appropriate lighting and a speed that lets you respond to what you can see.

title: Rain affects grip and vision
text: Wet conditions can change both traction and visibility. Rain can increase stopping distance and create spray that hides markings or hazards. Slow down, increase your space and avoid abrupt manoeuvres.

title: Never outrun your vision
text: You must be able to respond to what you can see. Fog, dust, darkness, rain and blind crests reduce the distance over which hazards can be detected. Speed must reduce with visibility when necessary.

title: Position matters
text: Knowing where your vehicle is helps you stay predictable. Be aware of your lane, the centre line, kerbs, crossings and nearby vehicles. Good positioning reduces unnecessary corrections and creates safer margins.

title: Fatigue is a safety problem
text: Tiredness can reduce alertness and reaction quality. Do not treat fatigue as something you can simply push through. Proper rest is the reliable response when you are too tired to concentrate.

title: Distraction can be mental
text: You can miss a hazard without taking your eyes off the road. Phones, conversations, eating, controls, stress and daydreaming can all reduce attention. Driving requires your eyes, hands and mind to remain available.

title: Prepare before moving
text: Set yourself up before entering traffic. Adjust your seat and mirrors, secure passengers, understand the route and deal with likely distractions before moving. Preparation reduces workload once driving begins.

title: Courtesy is defensive driving
text: Other road users will make mistakes. A safe driver expects late signals, missed observations, sudden stops and hesitation. Leave enough room that another person's mistake does not automatically become your collision.

title: See, plan, act
text: A useful driving rhythm is simple. First identify what is happening, then decide what it means, then make a controlled response. Early decisions are usually safer than last-second reactions.

title: Junctions are decision points
text: Traffic streams meet at every junction. Reduce speed as needed, read the controls and identify the traffic you must give way to. Do not enter faster than you can safely assess the situation.

title: Priority is not permission to rush
text: Having precedence does not remove your duty to avoid danger. Watch the other driver even when the rule appears to favour you. If someone is clearly not yielding, defensive action can prevent a crash.

title: Look before you commit
text: The critical checks happen before the turn or crossing begins. Look toward the traffic you will cross or join, check pedestrians and cyclists, and make sure your path is clear before moving into conflict space.

title: Turning right needs planning
text: A right turn can bring you across opposing traffic. Consider approaching vehicles, road markings, pedestrians and the space you will enter. Wait for a gap that allows the whole movement to be completed safely.

title: A left turn can hide a cyclist
text: The inside of a turn can contain vulnerable road users. Check mirrors and the area alongside the vehicle before turning. A bicycle or motorcycle can be close enough to disappear from a casual glance.

title: Give-way means prepare to yield
text: A give-way control tells you to be ready to let other traffic proceed. Slow enough to assess the road and yield when required. Do not treat the sign or marking as something to notice after you have entered the junction.

title: Stop where the stop control tells you
text: A stop line gives traffic a common stopping position. When a stop is required, stop before the line or at the location specified by the applicable control. Do not roll forward just because you cannot see another vehicle.

title: Do not block a junction
text: A junction works only when traffic can clear it. Do not enter an intersection or box when stationary traffic ahead leaves you unable to clear the conflict area. Blocking the space can trap cross traffic and pedestrians.

title: Traffic circles need a plan
text: Circles bring several traffic movements together. Read the signs, markings and lane arrangement before entering. Do not rely on a single memorised rule for every traffic circle.

title: Read the whole junction
text: One control rarely tells the entire story. Combine signs, markings, signal heads, lane arrows and traffic movement. The safest response comes from the complete layout.

title: A queue can hide a pedestrian
text: Stopped vehicles can hide people and traffic. Approach slow queues carefully, especially near crossings and junctions. Do not assume that the space behind a stopped vehicle is clear.

title: Do not gamble through a small gap
text: A gap is only safe if the movement can be completed without forcing others to react. If another driver would have to brake or swerve because of your move, wait. Patience is part of correct road use.

title: Emergency directions can change the normal flow
text: Authorised traffic-control directions must be followed. When a police or traffic officer gives a lawful instruction, obey it even when it differs from your usual route through the junction, while still proceeding safely.

title: Dead traffic lights demand caution
text: An intersection without normal signal control is a high-risk situation. Slow down and identify the applicable stop, give-way or other control before proceeding. Never assume the wider road automatically has priority.

title: Flashing amber means caution
text: Amber is a warning to proceed carefully. At an intersection, use due caution and apply the applicable precedence rule rather than treating the signal as a normal green.

title: Clear the junction
text: When your movement is permitted, do not leave the conflict area unnecessarily blocked. Continue far enough to clear the intersection unless another control requires you to stop. This keeps the road usable for other traffic.

title: Pedestrians are part of the turn
text: Your vehicle can cross a pedestrian's intended path when you turn. Check crossings and the side you are moving toward. A permitted turn still has to be completed without endangering people on foot.

title: Junction layouts can change
text: Temporary works and new signs can alter the normal pattern. Read the road you are actually on. Previous experience with the intersection is never more important than current signs and markings.

title: Do not overtake into uncertainty
text: A junction removes some of the information you need for a safe pass. Avoid a manoeuvre that puts you into a conflict area before you can see what is coming. Waiting is often the safest choice.

title: Traffic circles are not speed tests
text: A circle should be entered under control. Choose a speed that lets you observe, give way where required and maintain your lane. Carrying too much speed makes every decision harder.

title: Learn sign families
text: Recognising a sign family helps you understand its purpose quickly. Use shape, colour and symbols together. Then read the actual sign carefully so you understand the precise restriction, warning or information being communicated.

title: Warning signs are early information
text: A warning sign tells you to prepare for a hazard ahead. The useful response happens before you reach the hazard: adjust speed, position or attention so that the situation is already under control when you arrive.

title: Regulatory signs control behaviour
text: Regulatory signs tell road users what is required or prohibited. Treat them as part of the traffic control of the road, not as suggestions that apply only when traffic is heavy.

title: Information signs help you navigate
text: Information signs communicate useful route or facility information. They can identify destinations, services or road arrangements. Reading them early helps you make lane and route decisions without last-second movement.

title: Supplementary plates add conditions
text: A smaller panel can change how the main sign applies. It may give a distance, time, direction, vehicle category or other qualification. Read the whole sign assembly before deciding what it means.

title: Temporary controls can override habit
text: Road works can create a temporary road environment. Follow the signs, cones, markings and directions that are actually in force. Do not continue with the normal road pattern simply because you know it.

title: A restriction has a scope
text: A sign may apply to a particular direction, lane or section. Look for the point at which the control begins and any information showing where it ends. Avoid assuming every sign applies forever or to every movement.

title: Read signs early
text: The best time to understand a sign is before you reach it. Early recognition lets you change speed or road position smoothly. Waiting until the last moment can force unsafe lane changes or sudden braking.

title: Signs work with markings
text: Road signs and paint often form one control system. The sign may state the rule while the marking shows where to stop, which lane to use or which boundary must not be crossed.

title: Do not invent meanings
text: A familiar shape does not guarantee you know the whole message. Read the symbol or wording and consider the road context. Recognition should lead to understanding, not guesswork.

title: Signs can warn without requiring a stop
text: A warning sign and a stop sign have different functions. When a sign warns of a hazard, the response is normally to prepare and drive safely through the hazard rather than inventing a stop where none is required.

title: Direction signs should be acted on early
text: Route choices are easier before the junction than inside it. Choose the appropriate lane with enough time and space. Last-second cutting across traffic makes navigation harder for everyone.

title: Road markings are traffic controls
text: Painted lines and symbols organise movement on the road. They can separate traffic streams, divide lanes, mark stopping positions, guide turns and protect special areas. Read the road surface as carefully as you read signs.

title: A centre line separates opposing traffic
text: The centre marking helps keep vehicles on their correct sides. Crossing into opposing traffic needs to be both permitted and safe. A restriction shown by the marking must be respected.

title: Continuous prohibition lines mean do not cross
text: A continuous line can prohibit crossing from the applicable side. The restriction exists to control conflicts where crossing would be unsafe or otherwise not permitted. Do not treat it as ordinary lane paint.

title: Double prohibition lines reinforce the boundary
text: Two continuous lines make the separation especially clear. Where the marking prohibits crossing, remain on your side rather than using the opposing lane to overtake or turn.

title: Broken lines require a safety check
text: A broken line can permit movement when the circumstances allow it. The paint does not guarantee a safe gap. Check traffic, signs, road users and visibility before crossing or changing lane.

title: Lane arrows tell you how to use the lane
text: An arrow can show a required or intended direction. Read lane arrows early and choose your lane before reaching the conflict point. Do not cut across lanes at the last moment.

title: Stop lines mark the stopping position
text: A stop line gives vehicles a consistent place to stop. When a stop is required, stop before the line. Keeping the correct position protects the intersection and any crossing beyond it.

title: Pedestrian crossings need visibility
text: The crossing marks a place where people may be crossing. Approach slowly enough to stop when required and avoid overtaking in a way that hides pedestrians from you.

title: Yellow box junctions protect the intersection
text: A yellow box is there to keep the junction from becoming blocked. Do not enter the box when stationary traffic ahead means you cannot clear it. The box works only when drivers leave the conflict area open.

title: Road edges matter
text: Edge markings help drivers understand the usable carriageway boundary. Do not drift across the edge without good reason. Watch for pedestrians, cyclists and roadside hazards near the boundary.

title: Worn markings demand extra care
text: A faded line is still a reason to look for other controls. Use signs, road layout and surrounding traffic to understand the situation. When information is unclear, reduce speed and avoid risky assumptions.

title: Do not straddle markings
text: Lane boundaries are there to organise traffic. Keep the vehicle within the intended lane unless the manoeuvre requires a lawful crossing. Straddling lines can confuse others and reduce your own space.

title: A marking can guide a turn
text: Painted arrows and channelising lines shape the intended path. Follow the marked route rather than cutting across painted areas. Correct positioning makes your movement more predictable.

title: A marking can prohibit a movement
text: Not every road line merely divides space. Before turning, overtaking or changing lane, check whether a line prevents the movement. Continue until you reach a place where it is allowed.

title: Red means stop
text: A red traffic signal requires a stop. Stop at the applicable stop line and remain stopped until the signal permits movement. An empty junction does not cancel a red signal.

title: Green is permission, not protection
text: A green signal allows movement when the path is safe. Check that the junction is clear and that your intended movement will not endanger anyone before proceeding.

title: Amber means caution and preparation to stop
text: A continuous amber signal warns that the signal is changing to red. Stop when it is safe to do so rather than accelerating to beat the light. At intersections, follow the applicable caution and precedence rules.

title: Flashing amber demands due caution
text: Flashing amber does not mean normal unrestricted progress. Approach carefully, identify other traffic and apply the applicable rule for precedence at the intersection.

title: Do not enter a blocked junction on green
text: Green does not give you permission to block the intersection. Wait before entering if stationary traffic ahead means you cannot clear the conflict area.

title: Traffic lights do not replace observation
text: Signals control traffic but hazards can still exist. Watch pedestrians, cyclists, emergency vehicles and vehicles that may not obey the signal. A green light is never permission to stop thinking.

title: Lane arrows work with traffic lights
text: Some signal movements apply only to particular lanes. Position correctly before the intersection and follow the lane indication. Do not invent your own movement inside the junction.

title: A dead robot needs caution
text: When the normal signal control disappears, the conflict becomes more uncertain. Slow down and identify the applicable stop or other control. Do not assume the major road has automatic priority.

title: Stop lines keep the intersection organised
text: Stopping in one predictable place makes the junction safer. Do not creep across the stop line while waiting unless the applicable control permits movement.

title: Pedestrian signals protect crossing phases
text: People crossing can be less protected from a moving turning vehicle. Watch the crossing area when turning and give pedestrians the space required by the signal and road layout.

title: Emergency vehicles can change the situation
text: An emergency vehicle may approach even when your signal is favourable. Stay calm, observe its path and make way safely. Do not create another collision while trying to help.

title: Plan an overtake
text: An overtake is a sequence, not one steering movement. Check ahead, behind and the vehicle you intend to pass before moving. Make sure you have enough road to complete the pass and return safely.

title: Signal does not create a gap
text: An indicator tells others what you intend to do. It does not give you priority or make a poor gap safe. Check first, signal appropriately and move only when the road permits it.

title: Never overtake blind
text: You need a clear view of the area your vehicle will occupy. Blind bends, blind rises and poor visibility remove the information needed for a safe pass. Wait until you can see enough of the road.

title: Do not rely on the driver ahead to slow
text: The other vehicle may maintain its speed. Plan using real road space and speed differences. An overtake should still be safe if the vehicle ahead does exactly what it is doing now.

title: Junctions can make overtaking dangerous
text: Another road user can enter from a side road while you are in the opposing lane. Do not treat every clear-looking straight section as a safe overtaking opportunity, especially near intersections and crossings.

title: Pedestrian crossings change the overtake
text: A stopped vehicle can be shielding a pedestrian. Never use an overtake to pass a vehicle in a way that prevents you from seeing and responding to people using a crossing.

title: Return to the left safely
text: Completing the manoeuvre means getting back into the correct road position. Do not cut in so closely that the vehicle you passed has to brake. Make sure you are safely clear before returning.

title: Let the pass happen safely
text: If another driver wants to overtake, do not turn it into a contest. Do not accelerate simply to prevent the other vehicle from passing. Maintain a suitable position and allow a safe pass when conditions permit.

title: Following distance buys time
text: The gap ahead is part of your safety equipment. Leave enough room to react if the vehicle ahead brakes suddenly. Increase the distance when speed, weather, visibility or road surface makes stopping harder.

title: Reaction distance comes before braking distance
text: Your vehicle keeps moving while you recognise a hazard and begin the braking response. Distraction, fatigue and alcohol can increase this first part of the stopping problem. Better attention gives you more usable road space.

title: Wet roads need more space
text: Water can reduce tyre grip and increase stopping distance. Slow down and increase following distance. Avoid harsh steering or braking where possible.

title: A heavy vehicle needs room
text: Mass affects stopping and handling. Give heavy or loaded vehicles extra space and do not cut sharply in front of them. Your own vehicle may need more room when loaded too.

title: Do not tailgate
text: Following closely removes your margin for error. Even a good reaction may not be enough if the gap is tiny. Leave enough distance to stop without relying on the driver ahead.

title: Speed humps need an early slowdown
text: A raised road section should be approached under control. Reduce speed before the hump instead of braking hard on it. Controlled speed protects the vehicle and leaves you better prepared for hazards beyond it.

title: Curves hide information
text: You cannot react to a hazard you cannot see. Choose a speed that leaves you able to respond to what appears around the bend. The sharper or less visible the curve, the more conservative the approach should be.

title: Fog is a speed warning
text: Fog shortens your useful field of view. Slow down to a speed that matches visibility and leave more following space. Do not use the posted maximum as a target in conditions where you cannot see far enough.

title: Parking affects other road users
text: A parked vehicle can change the visibility and path of moving traffic. Before stopping, ask whether you will obstruct a junction, crossing, sign, driveway, sight line or emergency access.

title: Do not hide a crossing
text: A stopped or parked vehicle can conceal pedestrians. Keep crossing areas clear and avoid positioning where a pedestrian could step from behind your vehicle unseen.

title: Move off from the kerb carefully
text: Rejoining traffic is a change of position. Check mirrors and surroundings, signal as appropriate and move only when there is a safe gap. Do not assume a following vehicle will make room.

title: Opening a door is a road manoeuvre
text: A door can strike a passing cyclist or motorcycle. Check before opening, particularly on the side nearest moving traffic. A few seconds of attention can prevent a serious collision.

title: Animals need anticipation
text: Animals can move unpredictably on or near roads. Reduce speed when livestock or wildlife are nearby and avoid sudden steering that could create a different hazard.

title: Rail crossings require a complete exit
text: Do not enter a crossing unless you can clear it. A queue beyond the tracks can trap your vehicle on the railway. The space after the crossing is part of your decision to proceed.

title: A train cannot stop like a car
text: Rail vehicles need a long distance to stop. Never try to beat an approaching train. Obey the crossing controls and wait until the route is clearly safe.

title: Multiple tracks need multiple checks
text: One clear rail line does not prove the whole crossing is clear. Check all tracks and directions required by the crossing layout before moving.

title: Roadworks create temporary rules
text: Cones, signs and temporary markings can change the normal route. Slow down and follow the temporary arrangement. Familiarity with the old road layout is not permission to ignore the new one.

title: Potholes require mirror checks
text: Avoiding a road defect can create a lane conflict. Check surrounding traffic before moving around a pothole and avoid sudden swerves into another vehicle, cyclist or pedestrian.

title: Floodwater hides the road
text: Water can conceal holes, debris and damaged edges. Do not enter water that you cannot assess safely. Standing water can also reduce tyre grip and visibility.

title: Patience is a safety technique
text: Many risky manoeuvres begin with a desire to save seconds. Waiting for a better gap or allowing another road user to finish a movement often prevents the conflict entirely.

title: Carry the basic emergency equipment
text: Zimbabwe's construction and equipment regulations specify required equipment for applicable motor vehicles. For vehicles covered by the provision, this includes a serviceable spare wheel, an efficient jack, a suitable wheel brace or spanner, and the prescribed fire extinguisher.

title: Fire extinguishers have minimum requirements
text: The regulations specify different minimum extinguisher masses for light and heavy vehicles. A light motor vehicle requires a serviceable extinguisher of at least 0.75 kg, while a heavy vehicle requires at least 1.5 kg, subject to the regulations and applicable exemptions.

title: The extinguisher must be accessible
text: Emergency equipment cannot help if it is buried under luggage. The applicable regulations require the fire extinguisher to be approved and secured in an accessible and visible position within the cab.

title: Know your warning device
text: A stopped vehicle can become a hazard to approaching traffic. Zimbabwe's regulations prescribe a special visual warning device for motor vehicles. Learning how it is used is part of understanding roadside emergencies.

title: Vehicle equipment is a legal safety issue
text: Safety equipment is not only a comfort feature. The construction and equipment regulations contain detailed requirements for lamps, brakes, tyres, warning devices, wipers, indicators, loading and other equipment.

title: Brakes need more than a pedal
text: The braking system must be capable of controlling the vehicle. The regulations set braking requirements for different vehicle types. A vehicle with ineffective brakes should not be treated as safe simply because the pedal still moves.

title: Motorcycle brakes matter too
text: Two wheels still need effective braking. The regulations specify braking requirements for motorcycles based on their configuration. Brake condition is a basic part of safe riding.

title: Motorcycle helmets are required safety equipment
text: A motorcycle rider's head needs protection. Zimbabwe's construction and equipment regulations require motorcycle riders to wear the prescribed safety helmet. The rule is specific to motorcycle use.

title: Vehicle condition can create danger
text: A vehicle defect can make an otherwise legal manoeuvre unsafe. Check tyres, brakes, steering, lamps, wipers and other critical systems before driving, and do not ignore warning signs of failure.

title: Loads must be secure
text: A loose load can move, fall or obstruct traffic. Secure goods so braking, acceleration and cornering cannot make them shift dangerously. Loading is a safety task, not just a capacity task.

title: Overloading affects handling
text: Extra mass changes what the vehicle and tyres have to do. Overloading can affect braking, steering, suspension and tyre performance. Stay within the applicable mass and axle limits.

title: Towing changes handling
text: A trailer changes the size, mass and behaviour of the combination. Allow more space for braking and turning, check the mechanical connection and understand that the trailer follows a different path through a corner.

title: The correct licence must cover the vehicle
text: Zimbabwe's current driver-licensing framework uses coded categories. Do not rely solely on old informal class names. Know the code that covers the vehicle or combination you intend to drive.

title: Public-service driving has extra rules
text: Passenger transport is not always covered by a normal private-vehicle licence. Certain categories carry additional age, experience or other requirements. Learn the complete conditions for the category rather than memorising one number.

title: Alcohol affects driving skills
text: Alcohol can reduce judgement, coordination, attention and reaction time. A driver who feels confident can still have impaired driving ability. The safest decision is not to drive when affected by alcohol.

title: Drugs can impair driving
text: Impairment is not limited to alcohol. Some medicines and other substances can affect alertness, coordination, vision or judgement. Know the effect of anything you take before deciding to drive.

title: A phone can occupy three systems
text: Using a phone can take your hands, eyes and attention away from traffic. Zimbabwean traffic law restricts the holding or use of mobile communication devices while driving, subject to specified hands-free arrangements. The safest practical option is to deal with the device while safely stopped.

title: Hands-free still needs judgement
text: Removing the handset from your hand does not remove all distraction. Driving remains the primary task. Do not let a call or device demand attention that the road needs.

title: Fatigue cannot be negotiated with
text: Tiredness can produce slow reactions and lapses in attention. If you are too tired to concentrate properly, stop driving and rest. Short-term tricks are not a substitute for sleep.

title: Medication can affect alertness
text: Some medicines can cause drowsiness or blurred vision. Read warnings and get professional advice when needed. If a medicine affects your ability to drive safely, do not drive.

title: Emotions affect attention
text: Anger, fear and stress can narrow what you notice. If you are too upset to concentrate, deal with the situation before driving. Do not turn a road disagreement into an escalating conflict.

title: A driver remains responsible for attention
text: Passengers can create distraction but the driver must manage it. Keep conversations, noise and movement from interfering with safe vehicle control.

title: A breakdown is a traffic hazard
text: A stopped vehicle may be struck if approaching drivers cannot see it. Get as far out of the traffic stream as reasonably possible, make the vehicle visible and use the appropriate warning equipment.

title: A tyre blowout needs calm hands
text: A sudden tyre problem can make the vehicle pull or vibrate. Hold the steering firmly, ease off the accelerator and avoid harsh braking or swerving. Once speed is under control, move to a safe place.

title: Brake failure needs control
text: The first priority is to keep the vehicle under control. Stay calm, maintain steering, reduce speed using the safe control available and look for a safe place to stop. Avoid violent movements that create a second hazard.

title: Vehicle fire: protect people first
text: A burning vehicle can become dangerous very quickly. Stop safely if possible, switch off the engine and get occupants away from the vehicle. Property is secondary to life.

title: Crash scenes remain dangerous
text: A collision can create broken glass, leaking fluids and stopped traffic. Protect the scene and avoid standing unnecessarily in live traffic. Keep emergency access available.

title: Emergency vehicles need predictable drivers
text: Sirens and warning lights require your attention. Observe the emergency vehicle's path and make way safely. Do not rush through a red signal or create another hazard simply to clear the way.

title: Do not turn a minor crash into a second crash
text: Drivers may focus on arguments and forget moving traffic. After a collision, stay alert to surrounding vehicles and make the scene as safe as possible before dealing with other matters.

title: Call for help with useful information
text: Emergency responders work better with a clear description. Give your location, direction, number of vehicles involved and obvious injuries or hazards when requesting assistance.

title: Headlamps must work effectively
text: Vehicle lighting is part of both seeing and being seen. The regulations require motor vehicles to be equipped with prescribed lamps and kept in efficient operating condition. Keep lenses clean and lamps secure.

title: Main beam must not dazzle
text: Seeing farther is not useful if you blind another driver. Use the appropriate beam and dip when an approaching or affected driver could be dazzled. The purpose of lighting is safe visibility for everyone.

title: Rear lamps communicate position
text: Following drivers need to recognise your vehicle in time. Keep rear lamps and stop lamps serviceable so that your vehicle's position and braking are clear, especially in darkness.

title: Indicators communicate movement
text: A signal gives other road users useful information. Signal when required, but remember that the signal does not make an unsafe movement safe. Check the road before changing position.

title: Windscreen wipers protect vision
text: Rain can turn a small defect into a major visibility problem. Keep wipers serviceable so that water can be cleared effectively when conditions change.

title: Your windscreen must give you a useful view
text: A blocked or badly damaged view can hide hazards. Keep glass, mirrors and the relevant windows sufficiently clear for safe driving.

title: The horn is a warning device
text: The horn is primarily for gaining attention when necessary for safety. Use it to warn another road user when appropriate, not simply to express frustration.

title: The 2023 licensing rules use vehicle codes
text: Zimbabwe's current driver-licensing framework is organised around coded categories. The code on your licence determines what type of vehicle or combination you are authorised to drive. Learn the current codes rather than relying only on older class names.

title: Light-vehicle towing can need a combination code
text: Adding a trailer can change the licence category. Where the regulations require the combination code, the driver must hold the code that covers the towing combination, not just the base light-vehicle code.

title: Age requirements depend on category
text: There is no single age rule that covers every driving category. Ordinary learner licensing and professional or specialist categories can have different conditions. Always learn the complete rule for the category.

title: Omnibus driving has a specific age requirement
text: The 2025 amendment changed the omnibus and commuter-omnibus driver age requirement. The current provision requires a driver of an omnibus or commuter omnibus to be at least 30 years old, together with the other applicable experience and licensing conditions.

title: Experience can matter as well as age
text: Professional categories can require both eligibility by age and prior driving experience. Do not memorise only the minimum age. Learn the complete requirement attached to the licence category.

title: A driving licence is category-specific
text: Being licensed for one vehicle type does not automatically authorise every other type. Before driving an unfamiliar vehicle, check that your licence code covers it and any trailer combination.

title: Cyclists need predictable space
text: A bicycle has little protection in a collision. Give cyclists enough room and avoid squeezing past when the road is too narrow. Expect them to move around potholes, drains and parked vehicles.

title: Motorcycles can disappear in blind spots
text: Their smaller size makes them harder to see. Check mirrors and blind areas carefully before changing lane or turning. A motorcycle may be present even when the mirror looks clear at first glance.

title: Do not assume a motorcycle is far away
text: Small vehicles can be difficult to judge for speed and distance. Watch carefully at junctions and before crossing their path. Give yourself enough time to be certain.

title: Children require a slower approach
text: Children can move unpredictably near roads. Where children are present, reduce speed, improve your observation and expect sudden movement from between vehicles or toward the road.

title: Bus stops can hide pedestrians
text: A large vehicle can block the driver's view. Slow down and look for people emerging from behind buses or other stopped vehicles.

title: Pedestrian islands are not parking areas
text: A refuge gives people a safer place to wait or cross. Do not obstruct the island or drive onto it. Keep the protected space usable.

title: Animals can behave unpredictably
text: Livestock and wildlife may enter the carriageway suddenly. Slow down when animals are nearby and avoid sudden steering that could endanger other traffic.

title: Give vulnerable road users time
text: People outside vehicles have less physical protection. Do not hurry them with the vehicle. Patience, space and predictable movement reduce risk.

title: Use your left side consistently
text: Left-hand traffic requires consistent road position. Keep left on normal two-way roads and only cross toward the opposing side when a permitted manoeuvre or traffic control requires it.

title: Do not confuse left-hand traffic with hugging the kerb
text: Keeping left still requires a safe lane position. Avoid driving so close to the edge that you create unnecessary risk for pedestrians, cyclists, parked vehicles or road-edge hazards.

title: Scan far, then near
text: Good observation uses more than one distance. Look well ahead for developing hazards, then bring attention closer to your immediate path and check the sides and mirrors.

title: Do not stare at one point
text: Fixed attention creates missed hazards. Keep your eyes moving between the path ahead, mirrors, side areas and important road information so that your awareness stays broad.

title: A gap is useful only if it stays useful
text: Traffic spaces can close quickly. Before entering a gap, consider the speed of surrounding traffic and whether the space will remain sufficient for the whole manoeuvre.

title: Do not depend on another driver's signal
text: Indicators can be forgotten or misunderstood. Use other vehicles' signals as information, not proof. Check their position and movement before deciding what they will actually do.

title: Road position can communicate
text: Where you place the vehicle helps others understand your intention. Correct lane position, timely signalling and controlled speed make your movements easier for other road users to predict.

title: Avoid unnecessary lane changes
text: Every lane change creates another conflict point. Stay in the appropriate lane when possible and change only when the road layout or your planned movement requires it.

title: A calm driver sees more
text: Stress can narrow attention. Stay composed when traffic becomes difficult. Calm observation usually produces better decisions than rushing or competing with other drivers.

title: Do not let impatience set your speed
text: Trying to save seconds often increases risk. Keep your speed based on the road conditions and the information available rather than on how quickly you want to arrive.

title: Look for changes in traffic flow
text: Traffic patterns can reveal hazards before you see them directly. A sudden queue, braking wave or lane change ahead may indicate a hazard around the next bend or obstruction.

title: The first driver to notice a hazard has an advantage
text: Early detection creates options. Train yourself to recognise brake lights, pedestrians, roadworks and unusual vehicle movement before they become immediate obstacles.

title: Keep your vehicle predictable
text: Predictability helps everyone share the road. Avoid abrupt speed changes, unexplained lane movement and last-second turns when a smooth planned action is possible.

title: Observation is continuous
text: There is no single point where the road becomes 'safe enough' to stop scanning. Continue checking after a manoeuvre because conditions can change before the next decision point.

title: Approach a junction early
text: Good junction driving begins before the actual intersection. Reduce speed early enough to read the controls and observe traffic without needing harsh braking at the last moment.

title: Check the road you are joining
text: A clear path in front is not enough. Look for approaching traffic and pedestrians on the road you intend to enter before committing to the movement.

title: Turning right can expose you to opposing traffic
text: The movement may cross another traffic stream. Wait for a safe opportunity and complete the turn without forcing oncoming traffic to brake or swerve.

title: Turning left can hide a vulnerable road user
text: The inside of a turn is easy to overlook. Check alongside the vehicle and across the corner for cyclists, motorcycles and pedestrians before turning.

title: Do not stop beyond a stop line
text: The stop line gives traffic a common reference. When the applicable control requires a stop, keep the vehicle behind the line rather than creeping into the intersection.

title: Do not enter a blocked intersection
text: Your intended path includes the exit. If traffic ahead is stationary and you cannot clear the junction, wait outside it.

title: A junction needs space to work
text: Moving traffic needs room to cross and turn. Blocking one part of the intersection can create conflicts and gridlock far beyond your own vehicle.

title: Do not invent right of way
text: Traffic priority comes from the road controls and rules. Use signs, markings, signals and the applicable road rule instead of judging priority from road width or confidence.

title: Watch the wheels, not just the body
text: A vehicle may signal before it changes direction. The movement of its wheels and position gives useful information about whether it is actually turning or continuing.

title: Read lane arrows before the junction
text: Late decisions create conflict. Choose the correct lane early and follow the marked movement through the intersection.

title: A police direction is a traffic control
text: Authorised officers can direct traffic. Follow a lawful traffic direction carefully even when the normal signal or sign would suggest a different movement.

title: Do not follow another car into danger
text: The vehicle ahead can be wrong. Make your own assessment of the junction and its controls instead of copying an unsafe entry.

title: A stop sign requires a complete stop
text: The sign is not a suggestion to slow only. Stop at the prescribed position and proceed only when the road is safe and the control permits movement.

title: A warning sign asks for preparation
text: The hazard is ahead, not necessarily at the sign. Use the warning to adjust speed and attention before reaching the hazard.

title: A prohibition sign sets a boundary
text: Some signs tell you what must not be done. Treat the restriction as part of the road rules and do not rely on the absence of police to justify ignoring it.

title: Mandatory directions are instructions
text: Some signs require a particular movement. Follow the required direction for your lane or road rather than choosing the movement you personally prefer.

title: Read the entire sign assembly
text: Main symbols and supplementary information belong together. Check any plate, arrow, time period, distance or vehicle qualification before deciding what the sign requires.

title: Temporary signs can change the familiar route
text: Roadworks may make the normal road arrangement invalid. Follow the temporary signs and traffic-control devices that are currently in place.

title: Learn the meaning, not only the name
text: Recognition is useful only when it leads to action. Know what a sign means for your speed, position and movement, not just what the sign is called.

title: The road context can clarify a sign
text: A symbol is read together with its surroundings. Use the road layout, lane arrangement and nearby markings to understand how the sign applies.

title: Do not ignore signs because the road is empty
text: Traffic controls still apply in quiet conditions. A clear road can still have a legal restriction or warning that matters to your movement.

title: Read signs early enough to act smoothly
text: Last-second interpretation creates pressure. Give yourself enough distance to choose a lane, reduce speed or change direction safely.

title: A broken line is permission only when safe
text: Road markings do not remove judgement. A permitted crossing still requires a clear path, suitable conditions and compliance with other signs and rules.

title: A solid prohibition line is not an invitation
text: The line can restrict crossing. Remain on the permitted side rather than crossing simply because no vehicle is approaching.

title: Double lines deserve deliberate attention
text: Two continuous lines emphasise separation. Do not treat them like a normal dashed lane boundary.

title: A stop line is more than paint
text: It marks a controlled stopping position. When the relevant traffic control requires a stop, stop before the line.

title: Yellow boxes protect movement
text: The marked area is intended to remain clear when traffic ahead is stationary. Do not enter if you know you will be unable to clear it.

title: Lane arrows prevent guessing
text: The road can tell you where a lane is meant to go. Read the arrow early and select your position before reaching the junction.

title: Do not use markings only when convenient
text: A quiet road does not cancel them. Road markings remain part of the traffic-control system regardless of traffic volume.

title: Paint can be a safety barrier
text: Some markings separate conflicting traffic streams. Respect the boundary because crossing it can put your vehicle directly into a conflict path.

title: Stop before the line
text: A red signal needs a controlled stop. Brake early enough to stop before the designated line without crossing it.

title: Do not race an amber signal
text: The changing signal is a warning, not a challenge. Stop when it is safe rather than accelerating simply to avoid waiting.

title: Green still requires a clear path
text: The signal does not remove traffic from the junction. Proceed only when the intersection and your intended route are clear.

title: Watch for late vehicles
text: A favourable signal can still meet a vehicle clearing the intersection. Look in the conflict area before moving.

title: A dead robot creates uncertainty
text: Normal signal control may no longer be available. Approach slowly, identify the applicable stop or other control and make a cautious assessment.

title: Keep the crossing clear
text: Stopping in the wrong place can obstruct pedestrians and other traffic. Use the designated stop position and avoid occupying crossing space unnecessarily.

title: Read signals together with arrows
text: The same intersection can contain different movements. Use lane markings and the signal controlling your movement together.

title: Do not enter a junction you cannot clear
text: Green does not mean 'fill the box'. Wait outside when stationary traffic ahead prevents a complete crossing.

title: Overtaking needs a clear reason
text: Passing another vehicle creates additional risk. Only overtake when the improvement in progress is worth the manoeuvre and the road gives you enough space and visibility.

title: Check the road ahead before pulling out
text: The opposing lane can hide fast-approaching traffic. Do not move out until the distance and visibility are sufficient for the entire manoeuvre.

title: Check behind as well as ahead
text: Another vehicle may already be approaching from behind. Use mirrors and the appropriate blind-area check before changing road position.

title: Do not overtake near a hidden junction
text: A side road can introduce a new vehicle into your path. Wait until you have enough information about the junction and surrounding traffic.

title: Do not overtake where pedestrians are being protected
text: A vehicle slowing near a crossing may be reacting to people on foot. Never pass in a way that prevents you from seeing and responding to the crossing.

title: Return only when clear
text: The overtake is not finished until you are safely back in your lane. Leave enough space before returning so the vehicle you passed does not have to brake suddenly.

title: Do not accelerate to block a pass
text: Speed competition is dangerous. If another vehicle is overtaking safely, do not turn the situation into a race.

title: Night gaps are harder to judge
text: Darkness reduces visual information. Use extra caution when judging the speed and distance of oncoming vehicles at night.

title: Following distance is time
text: Space ahead gives your brain and brakes time to work. Leave enough distance to respond if the vehicle ahead stops or changes direction suddenly.

title: Increase the gap in rain
text: Wet conditions can increase stopping distance. Use more following space and a lower speed when the road is slippery or visibility is reduced.

title: Increase the gap behind heavy vehicles
text: Large vehicles can hide hazards and require longer stopping distances. Avoid following so closely that your view is blocked or your response time becomes too short.

title: Do not tailgate to stop another driver merging
text: A narrow gap can increase conflict. Preserve enough space to allow predictable traffic movement rather than trying to close every gap.

title: Braking starts in the mind
text: You must recognise the hazard before you can respond. Attention and observation therefore form part of the stopping process.

title: Poor tyres reduce your margin
text: Grip is essential for both steering and braking. Check tyre condition and pressure and replace unsafe tyres rather than depending on careful driving to compensate.

title: Park where others can see you
text: Visibility matters when a vehicle becomes stationary. Avoid positions that hide signs, pedestrians, approaching vehicles or junctions.

title: Do not park to block a crossing
text: A parked vehicle can conceal people from moving traffic. Keep crossing space and visibility available.

title: Do not use junctions as waiting bays
text: Stationary vehicles can obstruct turning paths and sight lines. Choose a lawful place that does not interfere with traffic flow.

title: Moving off from the kerb is a lane change
text: Rejoining traffic creates a new conflict. Check behind, signal when appropriate and enter only when the road is clear enough.

title: Opening doors needs a check
text: A passing cyclist or motorcycle can be beside your door. Look before opening into the traffic side.

title: Night stopping requires extra care
text: A stopped vehicle may be harder to detect. Use required warning and lighting arrangements and choose the safest possible position.

title: Check your tyres before a journey
text: Tyres are critical to control. Look for damage and serious wear and make sure pressures are appropriate for the vehicle.

title: Check your brakes
text: Brake defects can become emergencies without warning. If braking feels weak, uneven or abnormal, stop treating the vehicle as safe and have it checked.

title: Check your steering
text: Steering gives you the ability to avoid hazards. Unusual free play, stiffness or wandering should be investigated before continuing to drive.

title: Check the lights
text: You need to see and be seen. Make sure lamps and indicators work and remain clean and secure.

title: Keep the wipers ready
text: A sudden shower can destroy visibility quickly. Serviceable wipers help keep the windscreen usable in rain.

title: Know your vehicle equipment
text: The vehicle regulations cover more than the engine. Learn the required lamps, brakes, tyres, warning devices, emergency equipment and loading rules relevant to your vehicle.

title: A spare wheel is part of preparedness
text: A puncture can turn into a roadside hazard. Where the regulations require it, carry a serviceable spare wheel and the equipment needed to fit it.

title: Know the fire-extinguisher requirement
text: Vehicle regulations specify minimum equipment. For applicable vehicles, the prescribed extinguisher must meet the required minimum and approval conditions.

title: Emergency equipment should be reachable
text: Equipment is useless if buried under luggage. Store required safety equipment so it can be accessed when an incident occurs.

title: Loading changes the vehicle
text: Mass affects braking, steering and stability. Secure and distribute the load properly and remain within the applicable limits.

title: A trailer changes turning space
text: The combination is longer than the towing vehicle alone. Allow additional room and remember that the trailer does not follow exactly in the same path.

title: Check the coupling
text: A secure connection is essential before towing. Inspect the coupling and relevant connections before moving off.

title: Motorcycle safety begins with equipment
text: Two-wheel vehicles have little protection in a crash. Effective brakes, required protective equipment and good control are essential.

title: A motorcycle helmet is protective equipment
text: The rider's head is especially vulnerable. Zimbabwean regulations require motorcycle riders to wear the prescribed safety helmet.

title: Vehicle defects are not cosmetic
text: A damaged lamp, tyre or brake component can change the safety of the whole vehicle. Treat important defects as safety issues rather than minor inconveniences.

title: Learn the current code system
text: Zimbabwe's current driver-licensing framework uses coded categories. Match the code on the licence to the vehicle or combination you intend to drive.

title: Old class names can mislead
text: Zimbabwe updated its licensing framework. When studying for a current test, prioritise the current code structure and current amendments.

title: A trailer can change the licence requirement
text: The towing combination can fall into a different category. Check the applicable code rather than assuming the base vehicle licence is enough.

title: Professional driving has extra conditions
text: Passenger and heavy-vehicle categories can have additional requirements. Learn the complete category conditions, including age and experience where applicable.

title: Age is only one part of eligibility
text: Some categories require more than reaching a minimum age. Learn the full licensing requirement instead of memorising a single number.

title: A learner licence is for supervised learning
text: Learner status does not mean unrestricted driving. Follow the conditions attached to the learner licence and the training process.

title: Use the safest legal option
text: The best decision satisfies both safety and the rules. Do not choose an unsafe action merely because it seems faster or because another driver behaves that way.

title: When in doubt, create more time
text: Uncertainty and speed work against each other. Slow down and gather information before committing to a difficult manoeuvre.

title: Leave room for human error
text: Drivers, cyclists and pedestrians can make mistakes. A good safety margin gives you time to compensate for behaviour you did not expect.

title: Do not turn mistakes into arguments
text: Road conflict increases risk for everyone nearby. Give the situation space and focus on controlling your vehicle safely.

title: Good drivers keep learning
text: Passing an exam is not the end of road education. Review weak areas, correct mistakes and continue building sound habits after qualification.

title: Practice should test understanding
text: A question bank is most useful when it reinforces a real concept. Use different scenarios and wordings so the learner understands the rule rather than memorising one answer pattern.

title: Start with the road, not the test
text: Good driving starts with observation, judgement and control. The goal is not merely to memorise answers. Learn what the road is communicating, predict what other road users may do, and choose the safest legal action.

title: Zimbabwe drives on the left
text: Zimbabwe follows left-hand traffic. Keep your vehicle on the left side of the road unless a permitted manoeuvre, road marking, sign or traffic control requires you to move elsewhere.

title: The three-second scan
text: Keep scanning well ahead, then check mirrors and nearby hazards. Looking only at the vehicle directly in front of you gives you too little time to react to what is developing further down the road.

title: See, plan, act
text: A useful driving rhythm is: see the hazard, decide what it means, then act smoothly. Early decisions reduce sudden braking, sharp steering and last-second lane changes.

title: Speed is a decision, not a target
text: A posted maximum speed is not a command to drive at that speed. Choose a speed that remains safe for traffic, visibility, weather, road surface, curves, pedestrians and the condition of your vehicle.

title: Leave yourself an escape space
text: Avoid driving alongside another vehicle for longer than necessary. Keep a usable space ahead, to the side and behind so that you have somewhere to go if a hazard appears.

title: Smooth driving is safer driving
text: Smooth steering, braking and acceleration make the car easier to control and give other road users more predictable movements to respond to.

title: The safest driver expects mistakes
text: You cannot control what another road user will do. Drive defensively by allowing for late turns, sudden crossings, poor signalling, stopped vehicles and other human errors.

title: A licence means responsibility
text: Passing a theory test does not remove the need for judgement. A competent driver continually checks the road, the vehicle and the behaviour of other road users.

title: Keep your attention on driving
text: Anything that takes your eyes, hands or mind away from driving can reduce your ability to detect and respond to hazards. Safe driving needs continuous attention.

title: Mirrors are for planning
text: Check mirrors before changing speed, position or direction when traffic around you may be affected. Mirror use should happen early enough to give you time to adjust your plan.

title: Blind spots still exist
text: Mirrors cannot show every area around a vehicle. Before moving into another lane or position, check the blind spot as well as the mirrors and make sure the movement is safe.

title: Signal before the manoeuvre
text: A signal should tell other road users what you intend to do before your movement begins. Signalling does not give you priority and does not replace observation.

title: Do not signal and assume
text: Another driver may misread a signal or may not see it. After signalling, still check that the road is clear and that the manoeuvre can be completed safely.

title: Check before slowing sharply
text: If you need to slow substantially, be aware of traffic behind you and give appropriate warning where required. Sudden unexplained braking can create a rear-end collision.

title: Look through the junction
text: As you approach an intersection, scan for vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, signs, markings and traffic lights before you reach the conflict point.

title: Read the road early
text: Lane arrows, stop lines, signs and road markings often tell you what will be required before you reach the actual junction. Read them early and choose your lane in time.

title: A signal is not permission
text: Even a correctly indicated turn can be illegal or unsafe if the road marking, sign, signal or traffic condition does not allow it.

title: Think of stopping distance as two parts
text: Stopping distance is the distance travelled while you react plus the distance needed to brake the vehicle to a stop. Both parts become more important as speed rises.

title: More speed means less time
text: At a higher speed you cover more road every second. That gives you less time to recognise a hazard and less distance in which to correct a mistake.

title: Wet roads need more room
text: Rain can reduce tyre grip and visibility, so the distance needed to stop can increase. Slow down and leave a larger gap rather than relying on normal dry-road spacing.

title: Two seconds is a baseline, not a guarantee
text: A time gap is more useful than counting car lengths. Use a generous following gap and increase it in rain, darkness, dust, heavy traffic or whenever visibility is poor.

title: Do not tailgate
text: Following too closely removes your reaction space. Even if the vehicle ahead brakes safely, you may not have enough distance to stop behind it.

title: Heavy vehicles need stopping room
text: A heavily loaded vehicle, a large vehicle or one towing can need more time and distance to slow or stop. Do not cut in closely in front of such vehicles.

title: Descending changes the risk
text: On a downhill section your vehicle can gather speed quickly. Use a controlled speed before the descent becomes steep rather than waiting until you need heavy braking.

title: Curves hide hazards
text: A bend can hide pedestrians, stopped vehicles, animals, cyclists and oncoming traffic. Reduce speed before the bend so that you can deal with what you cannot yet see.

title: Never outrun your visibility
text: You should always be able to stop within the distance you can see to be clear. Fog, dust, darkness, crests and bends all shorten the distance you can safely plan for.

title: Overtaking needs a reason
text: Do not overtake merely because the vehicle ahead is slower than you would like. Overtake only when the road rules permit it and you have a clear, safe opportunity to complete the manoeuvre.

title: Before overtaking, check the whole manoeuvre
text: Look ahead for approaching traffic, road signs and markings, junctions, bends, hills, pedestrians and anything else that could make the manoeuvre unsafe.

title: Never force an oncoming driver to react
text: A good overtaking gap is one that leaves the oncoming traffic unaffected. If another driver would need to brake, swerve or make room for you, the gap was not safe.

title: Return to your lane smoothly
text: After passing, return only when there is enough space to do so without cutting in. Do not move back so close that the overtaken vehicle has to brake.

title: Road markings can control overtaking
text: A prohibition line or combination of lines may restrict crossing from your side of the road. Always read the marking before starting an overtaking manoeuvre.

title: Do not overtake at hidden conflict points
text: Intersections, blind bends, crests and other places with limited sight distance are dangerous because you may not see an approaching hazard until it is too late.

title: Keep to the correct lane
text: Choose the lane required by signs, markings and your intended movement. Do not use a turning-only lane to continue straight, or a straight-only lane to make a prohibited turn.

title: Controls come first
text: At a junction, obey traffic lights, stop signs, give-way signs, stop lines and give-way lines before relying on general priority rules.

title: Stop means stop
text: A stop sign or stop line requires you to stop before proceeding. A slowing vehicle has not satisfied a stop requirement merely because the road appears empty.

title: Give way means yield
text: At a give-way control, slow as needed and yield to traffic that has priority. Do not enter the conflict area simply because you believe the other road user can avoid you.

title: The right-hand rule
text: Where a junction is uncontrolled, the priority rule can give precedence to traffic approaching from the right. First make sure there is no sign, signal or marking that changes the situation.

title: Turning across oncoming traffic
text: When two vehicles approach from opposite directions and one wants to turn across the path of the other, the turning vehicle should yield rather than cut across the oncoming vehicle.

title: Do not cut the corner
text: When turning right, keep your turn controlled and avoid cutting across the junction. A proper turn keeps you predictable and away from the opposing traffic path.

title: Do not enter a blocked junction
text: Even when you have priority, avoid moving into an intersection that is blocked by stationary traffic. Entering without room to clear it can trap cross traffic and create congestion.

title: Read lane arrows at junctions
text: A lane arrow tells you how that lane is intended to be used. Follow the marked direction rather than changing your mind after entering the junction.

title: Traffic circles need patience
text: Give priority to traffic that already has the right of way in the circle and enter only when your path is clear. Look carefully for traffic approaching from the side that has priority.

title: A give-way sign overrides assumptions
text: If you are at an uncontrolled junction but a give-way sign or line applies to your approach, follow the sign or line. Do not use the uncontrolled-junction rule to justify entering first.

title: Y-junctions are about actual priority
text: Do not memorise a slogan such as “the base always goes first”. Read the signs, markings and movements shown at the particular Y-junction and apply the applicable priority rule.

title: Red means stop
text: A red traffic signal requires traffic facing it to stop and remain stopped unless a permitted signal movement or a lawful traffic controller instruction allows movement.

title: Green means proceed with care
text: A green signal allows the permitted movement, but it does not remove the need to check pedestrians, vehicles already in the junction and other immediate hazards.

title: Amber is a warning to stop when safe
text: Amber signals a change in control. Do not accelerate simply to beat the light. Stop when it is safe to do so and proceed only when permitted.

title: Flashing amber needs extra caution
text: A flashing amber signal calls for caution and careful observation of the junction. It does not mean “drive through without checking”.

title: Filter arrows control specific movements
text: A filter arrow can give permission for a particular direction. The arrow applies to the movement it points toward; it does not automatically cancel every other traffic control.

title: Police directions take priority
text: When a police officer or authorised traffic controller is lawfully directing traffic, follow the instruction given rather than trying to follow a conflicting signal at the same time.

title: Watch the whole junction
text: Do not stare only at the nearest signal head. Check your lane, the stop line and the junction so that you can respond to the signal change without panic.

title: A continuous centre line is a barrier
text: A continuous white centre line is used to restrict crossing. Treat it as a strong warning that the manoeuvre requiring you to cross it may not be permitted.

title: A broken line gives guidance, not permission for everything
text: A broken road line can allow a movement that a continuous line would restrict, but you still need to check signs, other markings and traffic conditions before crossing it.

title: Double prohibition lines mean no crossing from the prohibited side
text: Where double prohibition lines apply, do not treat the gap in traffic as permission to cross. The marking exists to prohibit the manoeuvre it controls.

title: A broken line beside a continuous line
text: When a broken line and a continuous line run together, the side on which you are travelling matters. The restriction is read from your side of the marking.

title: Lane arrows are instructions
text: Direction arrows painted on the road show the movement for which that lane is intended. Read them before committing to the junction.

title: Changing lanes is a sequence
text: Mirror, signal, check the blind spot, then move only when there is a safe gap. Do not signal after you have already started drifting across the line.

title: Diverging lanes
text: A diverging carriageway is one in which traffic lanes separate or split. Plan the required lane early instead of crossing multiple lanes at the last moment.

title: Dual carriageway basics
text: A dual carriageway separates opposing flows with a dividing strip or central reservation. Do not treat the opposite carriageway as though it were your normal oncoming lane.

title: Learn the sign families first
text: A strong way to learn Zimbabwean signs is to recognise their visual families: warning signs alert you to hazards, regulatory signs control road use, and information or guidance signs help you navigate.

title: Warning signs demand anticipation
text: A warning sign tells you that a hazard or change in road conditions is ahead. The correct response is normally to recognise the hazard early, adjust speed or position and prepare to act.

title: Regulatory signs control behaviour
text: A regulatory sign tells road users what is required, prohibited or restricted. Treat these signs as instructions, not decoration.

title: Give-way sign
text: A give-way sign tells you to yield to traffic with priority. Slow sufficiently to see what is approaching and be prepared to stop if necessary.

title: Stop sign
text: A stop sign requires a complete stop at the prescribed stopping position before you enter the road or junction. A clear road does not remove the stop requirement.

title: Speed limit signs set a maximum
text: A speed-limit sign sets the maximum speed for the controlled section. Conditions can require you to travel below that limit.

title: No-entry means do not enter
text: A no-entry sign prohibits entry from that approach. Do not treat an apparently empty road as an invitation to ignore it.

title: One-way does not mean fast
text: A one-way road controls the direction of traffic flow. It does not remove normal obligations such as speed control, observation, signalling and yielding where required.

title: Prohibition signs often use a red boundary
text: Red-bordered circular signs commonly indicate restrictions or prohibitions. Learn the symbol inside the circle as well as the shape.

title: Information signs help you navigate
text: Information and guidance signs communicate destinations, facilities, road layouts or permitted directions. Their job is to help you make the correct driving decision early.

title: Road-work warnings mean changed conditions
text: Temporary works can narrow lanes, move traffic, create uneven surfaces and introduce workers or equipment. Slow down and follow temporary signs and directions carefully.

title: Rail crossing warning
text: A railway crossing can combine limited sight distance, road traffic and a moving train. Approach under control, observe the crossing and be prepared to stop.

title: Slippery-road warning
text: A slippery-road warning tells you that grip may be reduced. Avoid harsh braking, steering or acceleration and reduce speed before entering the hazard.

title: Pedestrian warning signs
text: Pedestrian warnings mean people may be present or crossing ahead. Reduce speed and be prepared for a person to appear unexpectedly.

title: Animal crossing warnings
text: Where animals are likely to cross, reduce speed and watch both sides of the road. An animal can enter the carriageway with little warning.

title: Pedestrians are vulnerable
text: A pedestrian has no protective vehicle around them. Give vulnerable road users more space and time, especially children, older people and people who may have difficulty judging traffic.

title: Approach crossings ready to stop
text: When approaching a pedestrian crossing or an area where people may cross, reduce speed and keep your attention on the crossing area rather than assuming everyone will wait for you.

title: Children can appear suddenly
text: Children may run into the road, move unpredictably or be hidden by parked vehicles. Near schools, homes and play areas, reduce speed and expect sudden movement.

title: Cyclists need lateral space
text: When passing a cyclist, leave generous clearance and do not squeeze between the cyclist and oncoming or roadside hazards. The cyclist may need room to avoid a pothole or obstruction.

title: Do not intimidate a cyclist
text: Hooting aggressively, passing too closely or forcing a cyclist toward the edge increases risk. Give the cyclist enough space to remain stable and predictable.

title: Watch for motorcycles
text: Motorcycles are smaller than cars and can be harder to judge in mirrors or at a distance. Check carefully before changing lane or turning.

title: Never assume a road is clear because one lane is clear
text: Pedestrians, bicycles and motorcycles can occupy spaces that are easy to overlook. Scan the full area of the junction or crossing before moving.

title: Your vehicle must be roadworthy
text: A safe driver starts with a vehicle that is in a condition suitable for road use. Brakes, steering, tyres, lights, mirrors, visibility and other required equipment all matter.

title: Mirrors must give a useful rear view
text: The Zimbabwe construction, equipment and use regulations prescribe rear-view mirror requirements so that drivers have an adequate view of traffic behind them.

title: Clear windows are part of safety
text: A dirty, damaged or obstructed windscreen reduces the information available to the driver. Keep the glass clean and make sure wipers and washers work properly.

title: Lights are for seeing and being seen
text: Use the required lighting for the conditions. Make sure lamps and indicators are working and avoid dazzling other road users with inappropriate use of lights.

title: Check tyres before a long journey
text: Tyres are the contact between the vehicle and road. Look for damage, abnormal wear and inadequate inflation before travelling, particularly on a long or high-speed trip.

title: Brakes should be treated as a critical system
text: A brake problem is not a minor inconvenience. If braking performance changes, stop in a safe place and have the vehicle checked before continuing.

title: Do not overload the vehicle
text: Excess weight can affect steering, braking, stability and tyre performance. Load the vehicle within the limits for which it is designed and legally permitted.

title: Secure loose loads
text: A load should not be able to fall, spill, drag or shift in a way that creates danger. Secure it before setting off, not after it starts moving.

title: Passengers must not create a hazard
text: Do not allow passengers to obstruct your view, interfere with controls or occupy places that are not intended for safe passenger travel.

title: A breakdown triangle is a warning tool
text: When a breakdown creates a danger, use the prescribed warning equipment appropriately and get yourself and other road users away from the danger area where possible.

title: Never drive when impaired
text: Alcohol, drugs, illness, extreme fatigue and some medicines can reduce judgement and reaction time. The safest rule is simple: if your ability is impaired, do not drive.

title: Coffee is not a driving licence
text: Stimulants may make a tired person feel more alert without restoring safe judgement and reaction performance. Rest is the real remedy for fatigue.

title: Fatigue can look like poor concentration
text: Missing signs, drifting in lane, heavy blinking, forgetting the last few kilometres or struggling to keep your eyes open are warning signs. Stop and rest before the situation becomes dangerous.

title: Do not drive distracted by a phone
text: Handheld phone use can take your eyes, hands and attention away from the road. Do not make a phone conversation more important than controlling the vehicle.

title: A safe place is required for phone tasks
text: Navigation changes, messages and other phone tasks should be dealt with when the vehicle is safely stopped in an appropriate place, not while moving.

title: Strong emotions affect driving
text: Anger, panic and excitement can change speed choice, following distance and decision-making. Calm driving gives you more control over the situation.

title: Night driving reduces information
text: At night you generally have less visual information and more contrast between light and darkness. Reduce speed when necessary and make sure the road ahead is visible within the distance you can safely manage.

title: Avoid dazzling others
text: Use headlights so that you can see without blinding approaching drivers. Dip lights when required by the situation and keep dirty or badly adjusted lamps from creating extra glare.

title: Fog demands slower thinking and driving
text: Fog can make a familiar road feel suddenly unfamiliar. Reduce speed, increase caution and do not use a previous “normal speed” as your guide.

title: Rain changes visibility before it changes grip
text: Heavy rain can make road markings, pedestrians and other vehicles harder to see. Slow down early and increase your following distance.

title: Dust can erase the horizon
text: Dust, smoke and blowing debris can reduce visibility dramatically. The correct response is to reduce speed enough to remain in control and avoid overtaking into unseen traffic.

title: Standing water hides problems
text: A wet-looking patch can hide potholes, debris or reduced grip. Approach with care and avoid sudden steering through pooled water.

title: If a collision happens, think safety first
text: After a crash, protect people from further danger, stop as required, seek medical help for anyone injured and provide the information or assistance required by law and the circumstances.

title: Do not turn a breakdown into a second accident
text: A disabled vehicle can become a hazard to approaching traffic. Get it into the safest possible position, warn other road users and keep people out of the traffic stream where possible.

title: A puncture is a control problem
text: If a tyre fails while moving, avoid sharp steering and hard braking. Keep the vehicle controlled, reduce speed smoothly and move to a safe place when possible.

title: Brake failure needs calm control
text: If the normal brake system fails, stay calm, use whatever safe braking ability remains, reduce speed without violent steering and seek a safe place to stop.

title: A stalled engine does not remove steering obligations
text: If the engine stops, keep control of the vehicle, watch the traffic around you and move to a safe position as soon as you can do so without creating a new hazard.

title: Zimbabwe moved to code-based licensing
text: The 2023 Road Traffic (Licensing of Drivers) Regulations introduced a SADC-aligned code system and a correlation between the previous vehicle classes and the newer codes. Learners should learn the current codes rather than relying only on older class names.

title: Current licences use vehicle codes
text: The current regulations organise driver entitlements around codes such as A, A1, B, BE, C, CE, C1, C1E, D, DE, D1 and D1E, with additional requirements for particular vehicle categories.

title: Old and new systems can coexist in records
