text: The 2023 regulations include a correlation between old classes and new codes. This matters because an older licence may not be described using the same code terminology as a newer licence.

title: Public passenger driving has extra requirements
text: Passenger public service vehicle categories carry additional licensing requirements. In 2025, the omnibus and commuter-omnibus provision was amended to require at least five years of driving experience and an age of at least 30 years, with a transitional provision for certain already-authorised drivers.

title: A learner licence is not the same as a full licence
text: A learner or provisional entitlement allows supervised learning under the applicable rules. It is not equivalent to holding a full driving licence for unrestricted use.

title: Automatic transmission can matter
text: Where a licence or test carries an automatic-transmission restriction or endorsement, the driver must respect that condition. Do not assume an automatic test automatically gives unrestricted manual-driving entitlement.

title: Know what your licence actually authorises
text: Before driving a vehicle, confirm that your licence category or code covers that vehicle. Vehicle size, type, passenger use and combinations such as trailers can change the applicable entitlement.

title: Towing changes vehicle behaviour
text: A trailer increases length, mass and stopping demands. Turns become wider, reversing becomes harder and acceleration or braking may change noticeably.

title: Give trailers more room
text: Do not cut tightly in front of a vehicle towing. Leave additional space for braking and remember that the trailer can track differently from the towing vehicle.

title: Secure the coupling
text: A trailer must be connected using the required coupling and safety arrangements. A failed connection can turn a controllable vehicle into a serious road hazard.

title: Load distribution matters
text: A load that is too far to one side or too far back can change stability and steering. Distribute weight as intended and secure it before moving.

title: Learn rules as cause and effect
text: Instead of memorising “do this”, connect the rule to the danger it prevents. For example, a larger following gap gives you more time and distance to react when the vehicle ahead stops.

title: Pair signs with actions
text: For every road sign you learn, attach an action: identify the hazard or restriction, decide how it changes your driving, then act early.

title: Junction rules form a hierarchy
text: Think in this order: police or traffic-controller instruction, traffic lights, stop/give-way controls and markings, then the general priority rule that applies to the remaining situation.

title: Do not memorise isolated distances
text: A road rule can depend on the road layout, sign, vehicle type and exact circumstances. Learn the principle and the trigger, not an isolated number from a practice question.

title: A good learner explains the “why”
text: Being able to explain why a rule exists is stronger than recognising an answer option. When the picture changes, the explanation helps you adapt.

title: Use every drive as a lesson
text: When travelling as a passenger, practise identifying signs, lane arrows, traffic controls, hazards and likely actions. This builds road-reading skills before you are behind the wheel.

title: Double prohibition lines
text: Double prohibition lines indicate a strongly restricted section of road where crossing the marking for an overtaking manoeuvre is prohibited. Treat the marking as a restriction, not as a suggestion.

title: Reading a give-way-controlled junction
text: At a give-way-controlled approach, the vehicle facing the give-way control must slow and yield to the traffic that has priority. The diagram shows how that control changes the normal junction order.

title: Stop lines change junction priority
text: A stop line means the driver must stop at the marked position before proceeding. The diagram also shows that a stop requirement can exist even when the road layout itself provides no special priority for that vehicle.

title: Priority from the right at an uncontrolled junction
text: At an uncontrolled junction, where no sign, signal or marking changes the rule, traffic approaching from the right can have priority. The diagram illustrates how the right-hand vehicle is dealt with before the other vehicle.

title: Use the lane for the movement you intend to make
text: A lane marked for a particular movement must be used for that movement. The diagram shows a vehicle attempting to leave a lane marked for another direction, which would make the vehicle’s movement incorrect.

text: Railway crossings need an early reduction in speed and careful observation. The diagram reinforces the need to approach in a position that allows you to stop safely if a train or other hazard is present.

title: Turning across an oncoming vehicle
text: When two vehicles approach each other on the same road and one turns across the other’s path, the turning vehicle must yield rather than cut across the oncoming vehicle.

title: Traffic already in circulation
text: A vehicle approaching a traffic circle must consider the traffic already in circulation and yield where the applicable priority rule requires it. The diagram shows why an entering vehicle may need to wait before joining.

title: Warning versus regulation
text: A warning sign tells you a hazard is ahead; a regulatory sign tells you what road users must or must not do. Learn the action associated with the sign, not just its label.

title: One-way road
text: A one-way sign controls the direction of travel on that road. It does not mean that every lane or every turn is automatically available; follow the accompanying lane markings and other signs.

title: Speed derestriction
text: A speed-derestriction sign indicates that a previous speed restriction ends at that point. From there, the applicable general or newly posted limit governs the road, subject to safe speed for conditions.

title: Broken yellow edge marking
text: A broken yellow line at the side of the road is not the same thing as a centre line. Its meaning depends on the road-marking system and the specific road layout, so learn its prescribed use rather than assuming all broken lines mean the same thing.

title: Road signs and markings work together
text: A sign can modify how a junction or lane must be used, while a road marking can reinforce the same control on the road surface. Read both instead of using one and ignoring the other.

title: Do not rely on old licence labels alone
text: Older Zimbabwe driving materials may use class numbers that do not match the current SADC-style code system. For current licensing study, learn the new code structure and understand the old-to-new correlation where it matters.

title: Road safety beats speed of completion
text: A learner who understands ten rules deeply is building a stronger foundation than a learner who memorises fifty answer choices without understanding the situations behind them.

title: Seat belts are part of vehicle safety
text: A seat belt helps restrain occupants when the vehicle stops suddenly. Use the belt correctly and make sure it is properly fastened. A seat belt only protects effectively when it is worn as intended.

title: Check passengers before moving
text: The driver controls a vehicle carrying people. Make sure passengers are seated safely and that their behaviour is not creating a distraction or obstruction.

title: Insurance matters on the road
text: Using a vehicle on public roads is subject to compulsory third-party insurance requirements. The legal requirement concerns insurance or security for third-party risks. Do not confuse that minimum legal protection with comprehensive insurance.

title: Registration plates identify the vehicle
text: Registration plates are part of the vehicle's legal identification. They must be the authorised plates allocated to the vehicle and displayed as required. Homemade or misleading plates should not be treated as acceptable substitutes.

title: Keep registration information visible
text: Important vehicle identification must remain clear. Do not cover, alter or obstruct required registration information. The plate needs to be readable to other road users and enforcement authorities.

title: Know what the L plate means
text: The learner plate identifies a vehicle being driven under learner conditions. It tells other road users to expect a learner driver, who may be slower, more cautious or still developing control.

title: Learner status comes with conditions
text: A learner licence is not an unrestricted driving licence. The learner must comply with the conditions applicable to learner driving, including the supervision and vehicle requirements that apply.

title: Current codes map to older classes
text: Zimbabwe's 2023 regulations include a schedule correlating old classes with the new codes. This helps explain why older study materials may use different names. Learn the current code system first and use the correlation only to understand legacy references.

title: Code B and BE are different
text: The BE category covers a specified combination involving a light motor vehicle and trailer. Do not assume the trailer has no effect on the licence category simply because the towing vehicle itself is a light car.

title: Do not memorise professional rules from old notes
text: Licensing rules have been amended over time. Use the current regulations for age, experience and category requirements rather than relying on a number copied from an older question bank.

title: Know the difference between rule and advice
text: The Highway Code contains both safety guidance and matters prescribed by law. Treat legal requirements as requirements and good-practice guidance as guidance. Zivvvo should teach both without pretending every Highway Code recommendation is itself a criminal offence.

title: Why Zivvvo teaches the reason
text: Understanding the purpose makes rules easier to remember. A learner who knows why a rule protects visibility, stopping space or traffic flow is less likely to forget it when the wording of a question changes.

title: Learn the situation, not the sentence
text: Exam questions may describe the same rule in different words. Train yourself to identify the underlying traffic situation first. Then the exact wording becomes much easier to interpret.

title: One rule can appear in many situations
text: Road knowledge is transferable. The same ideas about visibility, stopping space, giving way and lane control appear at junctions, crossings, overtaking and parking. Learning the principle helps you apply it beyond one question.

title: Don't memorise a number without its meaning
text: Numbers are easy to mix up. Whenever a rule contains a measurement, age, mass or speed, learn what the number controls and what situation it applies to.

title: Legal minimum is not the same as safest behaviour
text: The law sets controls while good driving also requires judgement. A driver should never use a legal minimum as a target when conditions demand a more cautious approach.

title: Road courtesy improves traffic flow
text: Cooperation reduces unnecessary conflict. Letting another road user complete a safe movement, avoiding aggressive lane changes and keeping junctions clear can improve safety for everyone.

title: Every manoeuvre has three questions
text: Before moving, ask what you want to do, who could be affected and whether the space is sufficient. This simple mental check helps prevent hurried turns, lane changes and overtakes.

title: Build automatic checks
text: The best habits happen without a debate in your head. Mirror checks, observation, signal use and speed adjustment should become routine so that your attention can stay available for developing hazards.

title: A good learner asks why
text: The purpose of learning is understanding, not memorising answer letters. When you get a rule wrong, explain the reason in your own words. That makes the concept more likely to survive a differently worded question.
